body:
Matter is made of particles

Everything that has mass and occupies space is called matter. Water, air, iron, salt and oxygen are forms of matter. Although these substances have different properties, they are all made of extremely small particles.

The particle nature of matter helps explain why substances can mix, change state and undergo chemical reactions. To understand these processes, we must first distinguish an element from a compound and a mixture.

Elements, compounds and mixtures

An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom. It cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical reactions.

Iron contains iron atoms, while pure oxygen gas contains oxygen atoms. An element may exist as individual atoms, molecules or a continuous arrangement of atoms. For example, oxygen gas generally exists as O2 molecules, but it remains an element because every atom in those molecules is an oxygen atom.

A compound is a pure substance in which atoms of 2 or more different elements are chemically combined in a fixed proportion. Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen, represented by H2O. Sodium chloride, NaCl, is a compound of sodium and chlorine.

A compound generally has properties different from those of its constituent elements. Sodium is a reactive metal and chlorine is a gas, but sodium chloride is the familiar crystalline substance used as common salt.

A mixture contains 2 or more substances that are physically combined rather than chemically joined into a new substance. Its composition can vary. Air is a mixture of gases, and salt water is a mixture of salt and water. The constituents of a mixture can be separated by suitable physical methods.

FeatureCompoundMixture
CompositionFixed proportionVariable proportion
FormationChemical combinationPhysical mixing
PropertiesUsually different from constituent elementsConstituents retain their chemical identities
SeparationRequires chemical changePossible by physical methods
ExamplePure waterSalt water

Physical change and chemical change

A physical change changes a substance's physical properties, such as state, size or shape, without producing a new substance. When ice melts, solid H2O becomes liquid H2O. The chemical identity remains unchanged. Similarly, dissolving ordinary salt in water produces a mixture rather than a new chemical compound.

A chemical change, also called a chemical reaction, produces one or more new substances. Burning magnesium forms magnesium oxide. Rusting changes iron into iron-containing compounds. Browning food during cooking can also involve chemical reactions.

In an ordinary chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged into new combinations. The substances present before the reaction are called reactants, and the newly formed substances are called products.

Chemical changes may be accompanied by gas formation, colour change, heat, light or a precipitate. However, an observation such as a colour change alone does not prove that a chemical reaction occurred. The decisive distinction is whether new substances formed.

A physical change is often reversible, but reversibility is not the definition. Cutting paper is a physical change even though the original sheet cannot easily be restored.

Prelims focus

  • An element contains only one kind of atom.
  • A compound has a fixed chemical composition.
  • A mixture can have variable composition.
  • Melting ice is a physical change; rusting iron is a chemical change.
  • In a chemical reaction, reactants form new substances called products.
  • Trap: Oxygen gas, O2, is an element, not a compound.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class IX, Chapter 2, Is Matter Around Us Pure?, sections 2.3–2.4, printed pp. 19–22; NCERT, Science, Class VII, Chapter 6, Physical and Chemical Changes, sections 6.1–6.3, printed pp. 58–63.]

title: Matter, Elements, Compounds and Chemical Changes

body:
Why substances combine in definite ways

Chemical reactions produce substances with new properties, yet they follow definite quantitative rules. Two important laws describe what happens to mass during a reaction and how elements combine to form a particular compound.

Law of conservation of mass

The law of conservation of mass states that mass can neither be created nor destroyed in an ordinary chemical reaction. The total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products.

Antoine Lavoisier helped establish this law through quantitative studies of chemical reactions. During a chemical reaction, the atoms present initially remain present afterward, although their arrangement changes.

For example, when 5 g of one substance combines completely with 3 g of another substance to form a single product, the mass of that product is 8 g. If a reaction produces several substances, their combined mass must equal the combined mass of the reactants.

The law must be applied to the complete system. If a gas escapes from an open vessel, the remaining material may weigh less, but the escaped gas still accounts for part of the total mass.

Consider the formation of water:

2H2 + O2 → 2H2O

Before the reaction, there are 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms. After the reaction, the 2 water molecules together still contain 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms. No atom has disappeared or been created.

Law of constant proportions

The law of constant proportions, also called the law of definite proportions, states that the elements in a particular pure compound are always present in a fixed proportion by mass, irrespective of the compound's source or method of preparation.

Joseph Proust is associated with this law. Water always contains hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1:8. This is true whether the water originally came from rain, a river or another source, provided that the sample is pure water.

Consequently, if 3 g of hydrogen combines completely with oxygen to form water, the required oxygen mass is 24 g. The calculation follows directly from the fixed mass ratio: 3 × 8 = 24 g.

Ammonia provides another example. Nitrogen and hydrogen are present in ammonia in the mass ratio 14:3.

Water has 2 hydrogen atoms for every 1 oxygen atom, giving a ratio of 2:1 by number of atoms. However, the hydrogen-to-oxygen mass ratio is 1:8 because an oxygen atom is approximately 16 times as massive as a hydrogen atom.

John Dalton's atomic theory

In 1808, John Dalton presented an atomic theory that explained the laws of chemical combination. His principal ideas were:

  1. All matter is made of very small particles called atoms.
  2. Atoms were considered indivisible and incapable of being created or destroyed in chemical reactions.
  3. Atoms of the same element were considered identical in mass and chemical properties.
  4. Atoms of different elements differ in mass and chemical properties.
  5. Atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds.
  6. A particular compound contains the same kinds of atoms in the same relative numbers.

Dalton's theory explained conservation of mass because chemical reactions were understood as rearrangements of atoms. It explained constant proportions because a compound contains definite numbers of atoms of its constituent elements.

What modern discoveries changed

Dalton's theory was an important foundation, but not every original postulate remains valid in its literal form. Atoms contain smaller particles called electrons, protons and neutrons, so they are not indivisible. Moreover, isotopes of the same element can have different masses because they contain different numbers of neutrons.

Dalton's explanation of ordinary chemical reactions remains useful: the atoms of the reactants are rearranged to form products, without changing one element into another.

Long before Dalton, Indian philosopher Maharishi Kanad proposed the idea of extremely small particles called Parmanu. His contribution belongs to the history of philosophical ideas about matter; Dalton's theory was developed in connection with experimentally established chemical laws.

Prelims focus

  • Lavoisier is associated with the law of conservation of mass.
  • Proust is associated with the law of constant proportions.
  • Dalton presented his atomic theory in 1808.
  • Water contains hydrogen and oxygen in a mass ratio of 1:8.
  • Ammonia contains nitrogen and hydrogen in a mass ratio of 14:3.
  • Trap: Dalton considered atoms of the same element identical in mass, but isotopes show that their masses can differ.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class IX, Chapter 3, Atoms and Molecules, sections 3.1–3.2, printed pp. 31–34.]

pictures.caption: A balanced chemical equation represents the rearrangement and conservation of atoms.

title: The Laws of Chemical Combination and Dalton's Atomic Theory

body:
Chemical symbols identify elements

Each chemical element has an internationally accepted symbol. Symbols make it possible to express the composition of substances without repeatedly writing their full names.

The first letter of an element's symbol is always capitalised. If a second letter is present, it is written in lowercase. Thus, aluminium is Al, chlorine is Cl and cobalt is Co.

Some symbols come from historical names rather than modern English names. Sodium is Na, from natrium; potassium is K, from kalium; and iron is Fe, from ferrum.

Co represents the element cobalt, whereas CO represents carbon monoxide, a compound containing carbon and oxygen. Capitalisation can change the chemical meaning completely.

What is a molecule?

A molecule is a group of atoms chemically bonded together that can exist as an identifiable unit and retain the characteristic chemical composition of the substance.

Molecules may contain atoms of the same element or atoms of different elements. Oxygen gas consists of O2 molecules, each containing 2 oxygen atoms. Water consists of H2O molecules, each containing 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.

Atoms of some elements, particularly noble gases such as helium and neon, can exist independently as individual atoms. The familiar molecular substances are only one way in which matter is organised.

Atomicity of molecules

Atomicity is the number of atoms present in one molecule of an element.

  • Monatomic: Helium, He, and argon, Ar, are commonly represented as individual atoms.
  • Diatomic: Hydrogen, H2; nitrogen, N2; oxygen, O2; and chlorine, Cl2, contain 2 atoms per molecule.
  • Triatomic: Ozone, O3, contains 3 oxygen atoms.
  • Tetra-atomic: Phosphorus commonly forms P4 molecules.
  • Polyatomic: A common molecular form of sulphur is S8, containing 8 atoms.

Oxygen gas and ozone are different molecular forms of the same element. O2 and O3 have different molecular compositions and properties, but neither contains a second element.

What chemical notation tells us

The number written immediately after an element symbol, as a subscript, belongs to the formula of one particle or molecule. A number written before the formula, as a coefficient, tells us how many such particles or molecules are being counted.

  • H: 1 hydrogen atom.
  • 2H: 2 separate hydrogen atoms.
  • H2: 1 hydrogen molecule containing 2 atoms.
  • 2H2: 2 hydrogen molecules containing 4 hydrogen atoms altogether.

Similarly, H2O contains 3 atoms in each molecule, whereas 2H2O represents 2 molecules containing 6 atoms altogether.

Ions are electrically charged particles

An ion is an atom or a group of atoms that carries a net electric charge.

An atom becomes positively charged when it loses electrons and negatively charged when it gains electrons. A positive ion is called a cation, while a negative ion is an anion.

For example, Na+ is a sodium cation and Cl− is a chloride anion. The group SO42−, called sulphate, is a polyatomic ion because several atoms together carry a net charge.

Sodium chloride is an ionic compound. It contains Na+ and Cl− ions arranged in an extended structure. Its formula, NaCl, shows the simplest ratio of ions. It should not be interpreted as a separate NaCl molecule in the same sense as an H2O molecule.

Prelims focus

  • Element symbols are case-sensitive: Co and CO have different meanings.
  • Na, K and Fe come from historical names of sodium, potassium and iron.
  • O2 is diatomic; O3 is triatomic; P4 is tetra-atomic.
  • A cation is positively charged, while an anion is negatively charged.
  • SO42− is a polyatomic ion.
  • Trap: The subscript in H2 and the coefficient in 2H have different meanings.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class IX, Chapter 3, Atoms and Molecules, sections 3.2.1, 3.3 and 3.4, printed pp. 34–38.]

pictures.caption: A chemical subscript shows how many atoms of an element occur within one molecule.

title: Chemical Symbols, Molecules, Atomicity and Ions

body:
Why a special mass unit is needed

Atoms are far too small for their masses to be conveniently expressed in grams. Chemists therefore use the unified atomic mass unit, represented by u.

One unified atomic mass unit is equal to exactly 1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.

The isotope carbon-12 is assigned an atomic mass of exactly 12 u on this scale. Other atomic masses are expressed relative to this standard.

The relative atomic mass of an element reflects the masses and natural proportions of its isotopes. Consequently, an element's tabulated atomic mass need not be a whole number.

Atomic masses used in basic calculations

The following values are convenient rounded figures for school-level numerical problems.

ElementSymbolApproximate atomic mass (u)
HydrogenH1
CarbonC12
NitrogenN14
OxygenO16
SodiumNa23
MagnesiumMg24
SulphurS32
ChlorineCl35.5
CalciumCa40

Molecular mass

The molecular mass of a substance is the sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms present in one molecule of that substance.

For water, H2O, the molecular mass is:

2 × 1 + 16 = 18 u.

For carbon dioxide, CO2, the molecular mass is:

12 + 2 × 16 = 44 u.

For ammonia, NH3, the molecular mass is:

14 + 3 × 1 = 17 u.

Each subscript must be applied only to the element or group to which it belongs. For example, the 2 in H2O applies to hydrogen, not to oxygen.

Formula unit mass of ionic compounds

Ionic solids such as sodium chloride are not ordinarily composed of separate, identifiable molecules. Their formulas represent the simplest whole-number ratios of constituent ions.

The formula unit mass is the sum of the atomic masses represented by one formula unit of an ionic compound.

For NaCl, the formula contains 1 sodium and 1 chlorine. Its formula unit mass is:

23 + 35.5 = 58.5 u.

For calcium chloride, CaCl2, the formula unit mass is:

40 + 2 × 35.5 = 111 u.

Use molecular mass for substances represented by individual molecules and formula unit mass for ionic compounds represented by simplest ion ratios. Both are calculated by adding the appropriate atomic masses.

Atomic mass is not mass number

An atom's mass number is the whole-number total of its protons and neutrons. The atomic mass of an element, in contrast, is usually based on the weighted average of its naturally occurring isotopes.

For chlorine, the commonly used school-level atomic mass is approximately 35.5 u. This does not mean that a particular chlorine atom has 35.5 protons and neutrons. Individual chlorine atoms can have mass numbers such as 35 or 37.

Prelims focus

  • 1 u is defined as 1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.
  • The molecular mass of H2O is approximately 18 u.
  • The molecular mass of CO2 is approximately 44 u.
  • The formula unit mass of NaCl is approximately 58.5 u.
  • Mass number is a whole-number count of protons and neutrons.
  • Trap: Chlorine's average atomic mass of about 35.5 u is not the mass number of an individual atom.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class IX, Chapter 3, Atoms and Molecules, sections 3.2.2 and 3.5.1–3.5.2, printed pp. 34–35 and 39–40; NIST, Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions, Chlorine and column descriptions, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The molecular mass of water is obtained by adding the masses of its constituent atoms.

title: Atomic Mass, Molecular Mass and Formula Unit Mass
